lessons.title: What Is an API
lessons.concept: An API (Application Programming Interface) is a defined set of rules and interfaces that allows software components to communicate. APIs specify how to request services or data and what responses to expect, enabling integration between systems, applications, or services.
lessons.formula: Client sends request (endpoint + method + data) -> API processes -> returns response (status + data).
lessons.worked_example: A weather app calls a weather service API endpoint to request current temperature for a city and receives a structured response (e.g., JSON) with the data.
mistakes: Thinking APIs are only for web/HTTP (APIs exist at many levels)
Confusing API with the underlying implementation/database
lessons.provenance: Authored original lesson; not scraped. Requires independent verification before TRUSTED promotion.

lessons.title: REST Basics and HTTP Methods
lessons.concept: REST (Representational State Transfer) is a common architectural style for web APIs. RESTful APIs typically use HTTP methods to perform operations on resources identified by URLs: GET (read), POST (create), PUT/PATCH (update), DELETE (remove). Responses include status codes indicating outcome.
lessons.formula: Common: GET /items (list), GET /items/1 (read), POST /items (create), PUT/PATCH /items/1 (update), DELETE /items/1 (delete). Status codes: 2xx success, 4xx client error, 5xx server error.
lessons.worked_example: GET /users/42 retrieves user 42; POST /users creates a new user; DELETE /users/42 removes user 42 (subject to API design/permissions).
mistakes: Using GET for operations that modify state inappropriately
Ignoring HTTP status codes in error handling
Assuming all APIs strictly follow REST constraints
lessons.provenance: Authored original lesson; not scraped. Requires independent verification before TRUSTED promotion.

lessons.title: Requests, Responses, and Authentication Basics
lessons.concept: API requests often include headers (metadata, content type, auth tokens) and optionally a body (e.g., JSON). Responses return data and status codes. Many APIs require authentication/authorization (e.g., API keys, tokens) to control access and protect resources.
lessons.formula: Request: method + URL + headers + body. Response: status code + headers + body. Auth examples: Authorization header with token/key (mechanisms vary).
lessons.worked_example: A POST request with header Content-Type: application/json and body {"name":"A"} creates a resource; server responds 201 Created with the created object.
mistakes: Exposing API keys/secrets in client-side/public code
Not validating or handling error responses
Confusing authentication (who you are) with authorization (what you can do)

practice.question: What does HTTP status code 404 indicate?
practice.explanation: 404 Not Found means the server could not locate the requested resource. 200 is success, 301/302 are redirects, 500 is a server error.
